title: Photography & Movies
tagline: How people learned to catch light and make it move
intro: Have you ever wondered how a picture gets trapped inside a camera? For most of human history, a moment you saw was gone forever unless someone painted it. Then, about 200 years ago, inventors in France and England discovered how to make light draw by itself. In these 20 parts you will travel from a tiny hole in a dark room to the camera in your pocket. You will meet Niépce, who waited hours for the sun to make the first surviving camera photograph; Daguerre and Talbot, who raced to share their secrets in 1839; George Eastman, who put cameras into ordinary hands; and the dreamers who made pictures move, talk, sing and turn into cartoons. You will learn the real science of lenses, silver crystals, frames and pixels, see how photos changed news, families and history, and face the tricky question of whether a picture can lie. Grab your popcorn. The lights are going down.

outline.title: Light Through a Tiny Hole
covers: What a camera obscura ('dark room' in Latin) is: light from a bright scene passes through a small hole and makes an upside-down image on the opposite wall

The Chinese Mohist writings (attributed to Mozi and his followers, around the 4th century BCE) describing an inverted image through a pinhole, and Aristotle's notes on light through gaps during an eclipse
Ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen) of Basra and Cairo, around 1000 CE, and his Book of Optics that studied how light travels in straight lines using dark rooms
Renaissance Europe: Leonardo da Vinci describing the camera obscura, Gerolamo Cardano adding a convex lens (around 1550) and Daniele Barbaro adding a smaller opening for sharper images (1568)
Giambattista della Porta's book Natural Magic (1558) popularizing it as entertainment, and portable box versions artists later used to trace scenes
The big problem: the image was beautiful but vanished the moment the light changed; nobody could keep it
keyFacts: The camera obscura was understood for over 2,000 years before anyone could save its image
Light travels in straight lines, which is why the image through a pinhole is flipped upside down and left-to-right
Scientists, including Johannes Kepler in the early 1600s, used camera obscuras to safely observe solar eclipses
outline.hook: End with the question every artist tracing in a camera obscura must have wondered: what if the picture could draw itself and stay?

outline.title: Silver That Darkens in the Sun
covers: Johann Heinrich Schulze's experiment (1717, published 1727): he proved that silver salts darken because of light, not heat, by placing stencils on a bottle of chalk and silver solution
Carl Wilhelm Scheele (1777) showing that violet light darkens silver chloride faster than red light
Thomas Wedgwood and Humphry Davy's 1802 paper: they made shadow pictures of leaves on paper soaked in silver nitrate but could only look at them by candlelight because they kept darkening
The 'fixing problem' explained simply: unused silver salts keep reacting to light, so an image must be made permanent by washing them away
Drawing aids of the time, like William Hyde Wollaston's camera lucida (patented 1806), showing how badly people wanted accurate pictures
Introduce Joseph Nicéphore Niépce as a French inventor experimenting from about 1816, including his early paper negatives that faded
keyFacts: Wedgwood and Davy published in 1802 that their images could not be made permanent
Niépce and his brother Claude also invented the Pyréolophore, an early internal combustion engine that pushed a boat, patented in 1807
Niépce's earliest camera images on paper (around 1816) were negatives that could not be fixed
outline.hook: Close with Niépce deciding to try something completely different from silver: a sticky black tar that hardens in sunlight.

outline.title: Niépce and the View from the Window
covers: Niépce's process, which he called heliography ('sun writing'), using bitumen of Judea, a natural asphalt that hardens where light hits it
How it worked: coat a plate, expose it, then wash with lavender oil and white petroleum to dissolve the unhardened bitumen, leaving a picture
View from the Window at Le Gras (around 1826–1827), taken from his upstairs window at Saint-Loup-de-Varennes, the oldest surviving camera photograph
The very long exposure: estimates range from about 8 hours to several days, which is why sunlight hits buildings on both sides
Niépce's trip to England in 1827 and his failure to interest the Royal Society, partly because he would not reveal his full method
The rediscovery of the plate by historian Helmut Gernsheim in 1952 and its home today at the Harry Ransom Center, University of Texas at Austin
Niépce's partnership with Louis Daguerre (signed 1829) and his death in 1833 before photography became famous
keyFacts: The Le Gras plate is pewter, about 16.2 x 20.2 cm
Niépce also made a heliographic copy of an engraving in 1822 (later destroyed) and others in the 1820s
Niépce died in 1833, six years before photography was announced to the world
outline.hook: End with Daguerre alone in his Paris workshop, holding Niépce's notes and determined to make pictures in minutes, not hours.

outline.title: Daguerre's Mirror with a Memory
covers: Louis Daguerre as a showman and painter whose Diorama theater (opened in Paris in 1822) used giant painted scenes and changing light
The daguerreotype process: a silver-plated copper sheet polished like a mirror, made light-sensitive with iodine fumes, developed over heated mercury, then fixed with salt water (later hypo)
The breakthrough of developing a hidden (latent) image, which cut exposures from hours to minutes; label the 'broken thermometer' discovery story as a legend

François Arago announcing the invention at the French Academy of Sciences on 7 January 1839, the full method published on 19 August 1839, and France giving it 'free to the world' in exchange for pensions to Daguerre and Isidore Niépce
Boulevard du Temple (1838): the busy street looks empty because moving traffic did not register, but a man having his boots shined stood still long enough, often called the first photo of a person
Robert Cornelius's self-portrait in Philadelphia (1839), often called one of the first photographic portraits and a very early 'selfie'
Daguerreotype mania: portrait studios, head braces to keep sitters still, and each picture being a one-of-a-kind mirror-like image that could not be copied
keyFacts: The French government gave Daguerre a yearly pension of 6,000 francs and Isidore Niépce 4,000 francs
Mercury vapor used in developing was poisonous, which harmed some early photographers
By the early 1840s, better lenses and chemicals cut portrait exposures to well under a minute in good light
outline.hook: Finish by revealing that across the English Channel, a gentleman scientist had been secretly making a totally different kind of photograph, and the news from Paris had just alarmed him.

outline.title: Talbot, Negatives and the Race of 1839
covers: William Henry Fox Talbot's frustration sketching with a camera lucida at Lake Como in 1833 and his 'photogenic drawing' experiments on salted silver paper
The Latticed Window at Lacock Abbey (August 1835), the oldest surviving camera negative, about the size of a postage stamp
The calotype (from Greek 'kalos', beautiful), discovered in 1840 and patented in 1841, using a developed latent image and a paper negative from which many positive prints could be made
John Herschel's contributions: using sodium thiosulfate ('hypo') as a fixer in 1839, popularizing the words 'photography', 'negative' and 'positive', and inventing the cyanotype (1842)

Other claimants: Hippolyte Bayard in Paris (direct positive prints, shown in 1839) and his staged Self Portrait as a Drowned Man (1840) protesting his lack of credit; Hercules Florence in Brazil, who used the word 'photographie' in the 1830s
Anna Atkins and Photographs of British Algae: Cyanotype Impressions (first part 1843), often called the first book illustrated with photographs
Talbot's The Pencil of Nature (1844–1846), the first commercially published book illustrated with photographs, and the downside of his strict patents
keyFacts: Talbot hurried to show his work to the Royal Institution on 25 January 1839, less than three weeks after Arago's announcement
Daguerreotypes were sharper; calotypes could be copied many times. The negative-positive idea won in the long run
Herschel's hypo is still used as a photographic fixer today
outline.hook: End by asking: how does light actually change silver and glass into a picture? The next part opens up the camera to find out.

outline.title: Inside the Camera: Lenses, Light and Silver
covers: How a convex lens bends (refracts) light to focus a sharp image, and why moving the lens closer or farther focuses near or far things
The aperture (the opening) and the shutter (how long it stays open), and how together they control exposure; brighter light means shorter exposure
What silver halide crystals are and how light knocks loose tiny specks of silver to form an invisible latent image
Developer (turns exposed crystals into black metallic silver), fixer (removes unexposed crystals) and washing, step by step
Why film gives a negative (bright sky becomes dark) and how printing the negative onto paper flips it back to a positive
Simple at-home connection: make a pinhole viewer or a sun print on light-sensitive paper (with adult supervision and no chemicals that need special handling)
keyFacts: A smaller pinhole gives a sharper but dimmer image; a lens gives both brightness and sharpness
Photographers measure apertures in f-numbers; each full f-stop step halves or doubles the light
Grains in photographic film are microscopic crystals of silver halide such as silver bromide
outline.hook: End with the remaining problem of the 1840s: paper was blurry and metal plates couldn't be copied. What if you used glass?

outline.title: Glass Plates and a World on Camera
covers: Frederick Scott Archer's wet collodion process (1851), shared without a patent: glass plates coated, exposed and developed while still wet, with exposures of a few seconds
Cheaper relatives: ambrotypes and tintypes, and the craze for small cartes de visite (patented by André-Adolphe-Eugène Disdéri in 1854) traded and collected in albums
Traveling darkroom wagons and war photography: Roger Fenton in the Crimean War (1855) and Mathew Brady's team, including Alexander Gardner and Timothy O'Sullivan, in the American Civil War
The 1862 exhibition 'The Dead of Antietam' in New York, the first time many civilians saw photographs of a battlefield's dead (describe gently)
Nadar's portraits of famous Parisians and his balloon photographs (from 1858); the oldest surviving aerial photo of Boston by James Wallace Black (1860)
Art photography: Julia Margaret Cameron's soft, dramatic portraits, and stereoscope 3D viewers in many Victorian homes
Expeditions and landscapes, e.g. Carleton Watkins's Yosemite photos helping persuade the US to protect Yosemite in 1864
keyFacts: Wet collodion plates had to be coated, exposed and developed within roughly 10–15 minutes before drying
Because early plates were not sensitive to red or green well, skies often came out blank white and lips looked dark
Fenton could not photograph actual fighting because exposures were too slow and equipment too heavy
outline.hook: Close with the dream nobody could yet reach: photographing something moving fast, like a galloping horse, without a blur.

outline.title: Freezing Motion
covers: Optical toys that tricked the eye into seeing movement: the thaumatrope (1825), Joseph Plateau's phenakistiscope (1832), the zoetrope (William Horner, 1834) and Émile Reynaud's praxinoscope (1877)
Gelatin dry plates (Richard Leach Maddox, 1871), sold ready-made by the late 1870s, fast enough for exposures of a fraction of a second
Eadweard Muybridge's 1878 photos at Leland Stanford's farm in Palo Alto using a row of 12 cameras triggered as the horse ran past
What the photos showed: all four hooves leave the ground, but tucked under the body, not stretched out as painters had shown
Muybridge's zoopraxiscope (1879), which projected moving pictures drawn from his photos, and his huge study Animal Locomotion (1887)
Étienne-Jules Marey's chronophotographic gun (1882) that took 12 pictures per second on one plate to study birds in flight
keyFacts: Muybridge's horse was named Sallie Gardner, photographed on 15 June 1878
Marey's work helped scientists study motion and influenced early filmmakers
Dry plates meant photographers no longer needed to carry a darkroom everywhere
outline.hook: End with a young bank clerk in Rochester, New York, coating dry plates in his mother's kitchen at night and dreaming of making photography easy for everyone.

outline.title: You Press the Button: Eastman and Kodak
covers: George Eastman's start making dry plates (company founded 1881) and his switch to flexible roll film
The first Kodak camera (1888): $25, pre-loaded with film for 100 round pictures, mailed back to the factory for developing and reloading; slogan 'You press the button, we do the rest'
Transparent celluloid roll film (1889) and the patent fight with clergyman Hannibal Goodwin, whose 1887 application led to a court win against Kodak and a settlement of about $5 million in 1914
The Brownie camera (1900) for $1, marketed to children, and the birth of the 'snapshot' and family photo album
How snapshots changed daily life: holidays, birthdays, ordinary people keeping their own memories
New worries: the 1890 article 'The Right to Privacy' by Samuel Warren and Louis Brandeis, partly prompted by instant photographs and newspapers
keyFacts: Eastman invented the word 'Kodak' himself; he liked that it started and ended with the strong letter K
Developing and reloading the first Kodak cost $10
Roll film became the base for motion picture film, too
outline.hook: Finish by pointing out that a long strip of flexible film was exactly what inventors needed to capture not one moment but thousands in a row.

outline.title: The Race to Make Pictures Move
covers: Louis Le Prince's Roundhay Garden Scene (October 1888, Leeds), a couple of seconds long, and his unsolved disappearance from a train in 1890 (no conspiracy as fact)
Thomas Edison's lab and William Kennedy Laurie Dickson, who did much of the hands-on work: the Kinetograph camera and the Kinetoscope peephole viewer
35mm film with sprocket holes, developed by Dickson's team using Eastman film, still the basis of the film standard for over a century
The Black Maria studio (1893) and the first Kinetoscope parlor in New York (14 April 1894)
Max and Emil Skladanowsky's Bioscop show in Berlin (1 November 1895)
Auguste and Louis Lumière's Cinématographe, a camera, printer and projector in one, and their first public paid screening at the Grand Café in Paris on 28 December 1895
Edison catching up with projection: the Vitascope (designed by Thomas Armat and C. Francis Jenkins) shown in New York in April 1896
keyFacts: The Lumière program of 28 December 1895 had about ten short films, each under a minute
Kinetoscopes showed films to one viewer at a time; projectors let a whole audience watch together
Many inventors in several countries contributed; no single person invented the movies
outline.hook: End by asking how a strip of still pictures can fool your brain into seeing smooth motion, setting up the science part.

outline.title: How Movies Trick Your Eyes
covers: Frames: a movie is a long row of still photographs; explain frames per second

Why we see motion: the brain fills in movement between quickly changing images (apparent motion, sometimes called the beta movement or phi phenomenon); explain that the old 'persistence of vision' explanation is too simple
Intermittent movement: the claw or Maltese cross (Geneva drive) mechanism that pulls film down one frame, holds it still, then pulls again
The rotating shutter that blocks light while the film moves and flashes each frame two or three times to reduce flicker
Frame rates: silent films ran at varying speeds (often around 16–20 frames per second, hand-cranked), and 24 frames per second became the standard with sound
Nitrate film: bright and clear but highly flammable, and why projection booths were made fireproof
keyFacts: At 24 frames per second, a 90-minute movie has about 129,600 frames
A two-blade shutter shows each frame twice, so the screen flashes 48 times a second
Silent films projected at the wrong speed look jerky or too fast, which is why old films sometimes seem comical
outline.hook: End with early audiences who were amazed just to see a train or a wave, and a magician who realized movies could show things that never happened.

outline.title: Magic, Stories and the Silent Era
covers: Georges Méliès, a stage magician, inventing trick effects (the stop trick; label his 'jammed camera' story as a tale he told) and A Trip to the Moon (1902)
Alice Guy-Blaché, one of the first directors to tell fictional stories on film (La Fée aux Choux, around 1896) and later founder of Solax Studios in the US
Edwin S. Porter's The Great Train Robbery (1903) and new editing ideas; nickelodeons (first in Pittsburgh, 1905) costing a nickel
Filmmaking moving to Hollywood in the 1910s for sunshine and varied scenery; D. W. Griffith's influential techniques and the deeply racist The Birth of a Nation (1915), which caused protests
Stars like Charlie Chaplin, Buster Keaton and Mary Pickford; intertitles; and 'silent' films shown with live piano, organ or orchestra music
Lost films: nitrate fires and decay mean most American silent features no longer survive
keyFacts: A 2013 Library of Congress study found about 75% of American silent feature films are lost
A rare hand-colored print of A Trip to the Moon was restored and shown again in 2011
Nickelodeons spread to thousands of US theaters within a few years of 1905
outline.hook: Close with audiences watching a black-and-white world and wishing to see the red of a rose and the blue of the sky.

outline.title: Painting with Light: Color
covers: Additive color explained: mixing red, green and blue light; link to the three types of cone cells in our eyes
James Clerk Maxwell's 1861 demonstration of a tartan ribbon using three filtered photographs (taken by Thomas Sutton) projected together
Hand-painted and stencil-colored films, and the Lumière brothers' Autochrome plates (sold from 1907) made with dyed potato starch grains
Kinemacolor (1908, G. A. Smith and Charles Urban), the first successful commercial color motion-picture process, using two colors
Subtractive color explained: dyes of cyan, magenta and yellow absorbing parts of white light; Technicolor's three-strip camera with a prism splitting light onto three films (from 1932)
Disney's Flowers and Trees (1932), Becky Sharp (1935, first full-length three-strip Technicolor feature), and The Wizard of Oz (1939) switching from sepia to color
Kodachrome (1935), invented by musicians Leopold Mannes and Leopold Godowsky Jr., and Eastmancolor (1950) making color cheaper
keyFacts: Technicolor's three-strip camera was huge and needed lots of light, so sets were very hot
The last Kodachrome roll was processed at Dwayne's Photo in Parsons, Kansas, in December 2010
Color film did not fully replace black-and-white in Hollywood until the 1960s
outline.hook: End by noting color was arriving at the same moment as an even bigger shock: the movies were about to start talking.

outline.title: The Talkies Arrive
covers: Early attempts to join pictures and sound, from Edison's lab to Lee de Forest's Phonofilm (1920s)
Sound-on-disc: Warner Bros.' Vitaphone with big records synchronized to the projector; Don Juan (1926) with music and sound effects

The Jazz Singer (6 October 1927): mostly silent with a few synchronized songs and spoken lines, including Al Jolson's 'You ain't heard nothin' yet!'; note honestly that Jolson performed in blackface, which is recognized today as racist

Sound-on-film explained: the optical soundtrack, a wavy strip beside the pictures that changes how much light reaches a photoelectric cell, turning light back into sound (Fox Movietone, RCA Photophone)
Lights of New York (1928), the first all-talking feature, and the rapid switch: by around 1930 most Hollywood films had sound

Problems of the change: noisy cameras locked in soundproof booths, hidden microphones, actors whose voices didn't suit, and musicians in theaters losing jobs; Chaplin resisting dialogue in City Lights (1931)
keyFacts: Sound made 24 frames per second the fixed standard because sound must play at a steady speed
The first Academy Awards ceremony was held in May 1929
Vitaphone records played at 33 1/3 rpm, a speed later used for LP records
outline.hook: End with a small studio in Los Angeles that saw sound not just for actors, but for drawings, and a cheerful mouse about to whistle.

outline.title: Drawings That Move: Animation
covers: Émile Reynaud's Théâtre Optique (1892) projecting hand-painted moving pictures in Paris
Early cartoons: J. Stuart Blackton (1906), Émile Cohl's Fantasmagorie (1908), Winsor McCay's Gertie the Dinosaur (1914)
Cel animation explained: characters drawn on clear celluloid sheets over painted backgrounds (Earl Hurd patent, 1914), and drawing 12 or 24 pictures per second
Steamboat Willie (18 November 1928), created by Walt Disney and Ub Iwerks, famous for synchronized sound (not the first sound cartoon and not the first Mickey film made)

Lotte Reiniger's silhouette film The Adventures of Prince Achmed (1926), the oldest surviving animated feature, and Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1937), the first full-length cel-animated feature in color with sound in the US
Stop-motion: moving models one frame at a time, as in Willis O'Brien's King Kong (1933); and Disney's multiplane camera for depth
keyFacts: Fantasmagorie used about 700 drawings for roughly two minutes
Quirino Cristiani's El Apóstol (Argentina, 1917) was an earlier animated feature, but no copy survives
Snow White premiered on 21 December 1937
outline.hook: Close by turning from the cinema back to ordinary people, who in the 20th century were about to carry cameras everywhere.

outline.title: Cameras for Everyone, Everywhere
covers: Oskar Barnack's small Leica camera (sold from 1925) using 35mm movie film, making cameras pocket-sized and candid
Flash: dangerous magnesium flash powder (from the 1880s), safer flashbulbs (around 1930), and Harold Edgerton's electronic strobe photos at MIT freezing milk drops and bullets
Photojournalism: Life magazine (1936) and Dorothea Lange's Migrant Mother (1936); Jacob Riis and Lewis Hine using photos to fight slum conditions and child labor
Edwin Land's instant Polaroid camera (first sold in 1948), inspired by his 3-year-old daughter Jennifer asking why she couldn't see a picture right away
Home movies: 16mm (1923), 8mm (1932) and Super 8 (1965), plus easy cartridge cameras like the Kodak Instamatic (1963)
Photos from space: Earthrise taken by astronaut Bill Anders on Apollo 8 (24 December 1968) and The Blue Marble (1972)
keyFacts: The first Polaroid camera, the Model 95, went on sale in Boston in November 1948
Lewis Hine photographed working children for the National Child Labor Committee from about 1908, helping support child labor laws
Earthrise is often credited with inspiring the environmental movement, including the first Earth Day in 1970
outline.hook: End with a warning: as photos became everywhere and trusted, people also discovered how easily a photo could fool you.

outline.title: Truth, Tricks and Trouble
covers: Faked photos: William Mumler's 'spirit photographs' (1860s), the Cottingley Fairies (1917), made by two girls and admitted as faked in 1983, which fooled Arthur Conan Doyle
Political editing: officials removed from photos in Stalin's Soviet Union (for example Nikolai Yezhov), and propaganda films
Privacy and permission: paparazzi, surveillance cameras, and who owns a picture of you
Danger and waste: nitrate film fires such as the 1929 Glen Cinema disaster in Paisley, Scotland (71 children died in a panic caused by smoke), and chemical pollution from film factories and labs
Bias built into technology: color film long calibrated using light-skinned 'Shirley card' models, so darker skin was often shown poorly until improvements from the 1970s onward
Censorship and stereotypes in movies, such as the Hollywood Production Code (strictly enforced from 1934) and racist portrayals, and how this has been challenged
Photos as a force for good: evidence of injustice, science, and memory
keyFacts: The Cottingley cousins were Elsie Wright and Frances Griffiths
The Production Code was replaced by the movie rating system in 1968
Photo manipulation existed long before computers; it was done with scissors, paint and double exposures
outline.hook: Close by noting that, meanwhile, the movie theater faced a new rival: a box in the living room.

outline.title: Screens at Home and Spectacles in Theaters
covers: Television pulling audiences from cinemas, and theaters fighting back with widescreen (Cinerama 1952, CinemaScope with The Robe in 1953) and 1950s 3D movies
Videotape: Ampex's recorder (1956) for TV, then home VHS and Betamax (mid-1970s) and the first consumer camcorders (1980s)
IMAX: first shown at Expo '70 in Osaka, Japan, using huge 70mm film frames running sideways
Special effects: Star Wars (1977) and Industrial Light & Magic's computer-controlled motion-control camera
Computer graphics in films: Tron (1982), the first fully computer-generated character in Young Sherlock Holmes (1985), dinosaurs in Jurassic Park (1993)
Toy Story (1995) by Pixar, the first fully computer-animated feature film
keyFacts: Sony's Betamax launched in 1975 and JVC's VHS in 1976; VHS eventually won the format war
Toy Story was released in November 1995
An IMAX film frame is about ten times larger than a standard 35mm frame
outline.hook: End by hinting that while Hollywood used computers for effects, a Kodak engineer had already built a camera with no film at all.

outline.title: Pictures Made of Numbers
covers: Russell Kirsch's 1957 scan of a photo of his baby son Walden, one of the first digital images (176 x 176 pixels)

The CCD image sensor invented at Bell Labs in 1969 by Willard Boyle and George E. Smith (Nobel Prize in Physics 2009), and later CMOS sensors developed by Eric Fossum's team at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in the 1990s

How a sensor works: millions of pixels turn light into electric charge, counted as numbers; Bryce Bayer's color filter pattern (Kodak, 1976) with twice as many green filters because our eyes are most sensitive to green
Steven Sasson's prototype at Kodak (1975): about 3.6 kg, 0.01 megapixels, 23 seconds to record one black-and-white image to a cassette tape

From analog still video (Sony Mavica, announced 1981) to the first consumer digital cameras (Dycam Model 1 / Logitech Fotoman, 1990), the Kodak DCS 100 for professionals (1991) and the JPEG standard (1992)
Digital cinema: Star Wars: Episode II (2002) shot on digital video, and theaters mostly switching to digital projectors by the early 2010s
Kodak's struggle and bankruptcy filing in January 2012, and why the story is more complicated than 'they ignored digital'
keyFacts: 1 megapixel = 1 million pixels; Sasson's camera had 10,000
Digital photos can be copied endlessly with no loss, unlike film
Kodak sold many digital cameras in the 2000s but profits from film disappeared fast
outline.hook: Finish with a phone ringing in 2000 in Japan, a phone that could also take a picture.

outline.title: Every Pocket a Studio, and Tomorrow's Pictures
covers: Camera phones: Philippe Kahn sharing a photo of his newborn daughter from his phone (1997), the Sharp J-SH04 in Japan (2000), and the iPhone (2007) with a 2-megapixel camera
Sharing: YouTube's first video 'Me at the zoo' (23 April 2005), Instagram (2010), selfies, and video making everyone a filmmaker; the film Tangerine (2015) shot on iPhones
Computational photography: phones combining many quick shots for night mode, HDR and portrait blur
Pictures beyond human eyes: Hubble (1990), the first image of a black hole (Event Horizon Telescope, 2019) and the James Webb Space Telescope's first images (2022)

The future, labeled as possibilities: AI-generated images and video, deepfakes, 'content credentials' that record where a photo came from, LED-wall virtual sets, VR and 3D capture; some directors and artists still choose real film
Tie everything together: from the pinhole to the pixel, the same idea of catching light, plus a final thought about using photos honestly and kindly
keyFacts: Researchers estimate more than a trillion photos are now taken each year, most on phones
The Event Horizon Telescope image of the black hole M87* was released on 10 April 2019
Every phone camera still uses a lens, an aperture and a light-sensitive surface, ideas that go back to the camera obscura
outline.hook: End the whole Deep Dive by inviting the reader to go take a picture and remember they're holding 2,000 years of invention.

glossary: camera obscura — a dark room or box where light through a small hole projects an upside-down image
lens — a curved piece of glass that bends light to make a sharp, bright image
aperture — the opening that controls how much light enters a camera
shutter — the part that opens and closes to let light in for a set time
exposure — the total amount of light that reaches the film or sensor
silver halide — light-sensitive crystals of silver combined with chlorine, bromine or iodine, used in film
latent image — an invisible picture formed by light that appears only after developing
developer — a chemical that turns the latent image into a visible one
fixer (hypo) — a chemical that removes unused light-sensitive silver so the picture stops changing
negative — an image with light and dark reversed, used to print many positive copies
daguerreotype — a one-of-a-kind photograph on a polished silver-coated copper plate
calotype — Talbot's paper negative process that allowed many prints
wet collodion — a process using glass plates coated with sticky collodion that had to stay wet
frames per second (fps) — how many still pictures (frames) are shown each second
sprocket holes — the small holes along film edges that let gears move it precisely
optical soundtrack — a strip beside movie frames that stores sound as patterns of light
additive color — making colors by mixing red, green and blue light
subtractive color — making colors with cyan, magenta and yellow dyes that absorb parts of white light
pixel — one tiny square of a digital picture that records a single color and brightness
image sensor (CCD/CMOS) — the chip in a digital camera that turns light into electrical signals
doNotSay: Do not say Daguerre invented the first photograph; Niépce's Le Gras image (around 1826–1827) is older
Do not say one person 'invented photography' or 'invented the movies'; many people in several countries contributed
Do not say Leonardo da Vinci invented the camera obscura; it was known for many centuries before him
Do not give the Le Gras exposure as exactly 8 hours; say 'hours, possibly days'
Do not say people in old photos never smiled only because exposures were long; customs and portrait traditions also mattered, and by the 1840s exposures were often under a minute
Do not say Edison single-handedly invented motion pictures; Dickson did much of the work and others worked in parallel
Do not state as fact that audiences ran screaming from the Lumière train film; it is a popular legend with little evidence
Do not state as fact that Leland Stanford made a $25,000 bet about the horse; that story is a legend
Do not state as fact that Edison or anyone else murdered Louis Le Prince; his disappearance is unsolved
Do not say movies work only because of 'persistence of vision'; the brain's perception of apparent motion is the better explanation
Do not say The Jazz Singer was the first sound film or was fully talking; it was mostly silent with some synchronized sequences
Do not say Steamboat Willie was the first sound cartoon or the first Mickey Mouse cartoon made
Do not say Snow White was the first animated feature ever; earlier ones existed, e.g. El Apóstol (1917, lost) and Prince Achmed (1926)
Do not say The Wizard of Oz was the first color film
Do not say silent films were watched in silence; they usually had live music
Do not say Kodak invented digital photography and simply hid it; the real story of Kodak's decline is more complicated
Do not say the name 'Kodak' has a hidden meaning or comes from a camera sound; Eastman made it up
Do not say photographs always show the truth; photos have been staged and edited since the 1800s
Do not say Vermeer definitely used a camera obscura; historians still debate it
Do not present future technologies as certain; label them as possibilities
